**TL;DR: this article is about how I convinced myself to be a Bayesian. Note that Frequentist vs Bayesian is a common debate amongst statisticians.**

My undergraduate prince (c)harming (now ex) was determined to challenge me on everything I believed in. He was incredibly skilled at arguing and usually had better answers for almost everything, and I usually depended on him for things I didn't know. He left one question for me to answer: how did I benefit him in our relationship? I never found a sufficient answer for him. Due to my insecurities, I did things I shouldn’t have and I contributed to the dramatic end of our relationship.

At the start of undergrad, I decided to go vegan for ethical reasons, and I was determined to stick with it. I believed in living that lifestyle—and still do. To stay resolute, I became obsessed with watching vegan debate videos. These two experiences—going vegan and frequently debating in my past relationship—shaped me into someone who can argue.

I’ve always enjoyed shouting weird phrases in ways that catch people’s attention, crafting sentences that even generative AI can never form. One early morning, as the sun was just rising on a random Wednesday, I spontaneously made an obscure comparison to my graduate school sweetheart: “Being Bayesian is like being vegan.”

Wanting to push the analogy further, I continued, “People will tell you that being Bayesian is too computationally expensive… but really, with modern computers, it’s not an excuse.”

My voice rising, I added, “And everyone swears by frequentist methods because that’s how we started, and it’s what we’ve always done—just like people eat meat because they were born into families that eat meat. But that doesn’t necessarily mean Bayesian methods are bad!

There’s so much evidence for why we should adopt Bayesian approaches. First, we can probably all agree that frequentist hypothesis testing is flawed and that p-values are widely misunderstood. A simple null hypothesis—the foundation of most common tests—is almost never true. The probability of obtaining a statistic that exactly matches the null hypothesis is incredibly low.

Second, the complete class theorem (Ferguson, 1967) demonstrates that for any procedure, there exists a better Bayesian alternative. Bayesian statistics is also more general: frequentist methods assume that population parameters are fixed, while Bayesian methods do not! The only fixed element in Bayesian statistics is the prior you choose to use (from my understanding…)

Critics often say Bayesian statistics is ‘more subjective,’ but frequentist models come with their own assumptions—assumptions that often don’t hold. For instance, many people claim their data follows a normal distribution when it doesn’t. As the saying goes, all models are wrong, but Bayesian ones have the flexibility to pull us closer to the truth.

Ultimately, the main reason people stick with frequentist methods is convenience. And just because something is easier doesn’t mean it’s the best approach.”

I’m not going to delve into the details of how this is analogous to arguments for veganism, but if you genuinely consider why people choose to go vegan, you’ll understand. I also recognize that veganism is fundamentally a moral issue. But similarly, if you care about pursuing true knowledge in academia, there’s something troubling about modeling data incorrectly.

That said, I’m still not a true Bayesian. There are times when I will use frequentist methods simply because they’re universally accepted and required for certain situations, and I am ashamed of it! I aspire to improve my statistical skills and, one day, consistently employ Bayesian approaches—even for simple tests such as the comparisons of means between two groups. (That being said, you may need to be a frequentist so you don't get fired from your career.)

I may cringe at this piece in the future—and that would be a good thing! It would mean I’ve grown and learned. But for now, I’ve accidentally convinced myself to become a Bayesian. Such is the curse of learning how to argue.
